note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §8, §13.7, Stage 71; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiment 26) on data/benches/heating_curve.json: ice's heat of fusion by a calorimeter (two ice cubes into warm water in a foam cup), then a heating curve (crushed ice from the freezer heated and stirred, its temperature logged): the plateau at 0 C while it melts, the rise, the plateau at 100 C while it boils.
title: Experiment: a heating curve and the heat of fusion

steps.title: Your guess
steps.text: Melting ice takes heat without warming it. How many joules do you think it takes to melt one gram of ice? (Warming a gram of water by one degree takes 4.18 J.) Type your guess, then click "predict".
steps.why: Heat that goes into melting pulls the ice's molecules out of their crystal; it does not make them move faster, so the temperature does not change while it happens. That heat is the heat of fusion.

steps.title: Log the cup's temperature
steps.text: Right-click the foam cup, click "+ T", open the notebook and click "5 s".
steps.why: The cup holds 100 g of water at 40 C. Foam lets little heat through, so what the water gives up goes into whatever is put in it.

steps.title: The ice into the cup
steps.text: Close the notebook. Pick up the jar of ice cubes, then right-click the cup. In the menu that opens, click "tip in".
steps.why: The jar holds two ice cubes, 20 g, at 0 C.

steps.title: Stir the cup
steps.why: Stirred, the warm water keeps reaching the ice and it melts in a minute or two: little heat leaks in or out of the cup meanwhile.

steps.title: Until they are gone
steps.text: Watch the cup's temperature fall as the ice melts.
steps.why: The warm water gives up its heat: first to melt the ice, then to warm the ice's water up to its own temperature. 100 g of water falling by a degree gives up 418 J.

checks.text: no ice left in the cup

steps.title: Log the ice's temperature
steps.text: Right-click the beaker of crushed ice, click "+ T", open the notebook and click "5 s".
steps.why: The beaker holds 100 g of crushed ice from the freezer, at -10 C.

steps.title: The burner under it
steps.text: Close the notebook. Drag the burner from Supplies onto the beaker of ice.

checks.text: the burner is under the ice

steps.title: A gentle flame
steps.text: Choose the burner and open its valve halfway.

steps.title: Speed up time
steps.text: Click "10x" at the top, and open the notebook to watch the curve.

checks.text: time runs at least 10 times faster
the ice at its melting point, some melted

steps.title: Stir it
steps.text: Now some of it is water: choose the beaker, then "stir".
steps.why: Stirred, the beaker is one temperature throughout: the curve is the whole beaker's.

steps.title: The first plateau
steps.text: While it melts the line is flat at 0 C, though the burner never stops.
steps.why: Every joule the flame gives goes into melting, none into warming, until the last of the ice is gone: the line stands still at the melting point.

steps.title: The rise, and the second plateau
steps.text: Now the water warms, steadily, to 100 C, and boils.
steps.why: Boiling holds it at 100 C as melting held it at 0 C: the flame's heat goes into turning water to steam. That plateau is far longer than the first: boiling a gram of water takes about seven times what melting a gram of ice does.

steps.title: The burner off
steps.text: Choose the burner and shut its valve, before it boils dry.

fails.text: The beaker boiled dry: its glass is far hotter than any plateau now. Press reset to start again.

goal.text: every element, mass and energy unchanged

report.label: the heat to melt a gram of ice
report.why: From the notebook: the cup fell from its start to its least. The water gave up 100 g x 4.18 J/g K x that fall; of it, the ice's own 20 g took 20 g x 4.18 J/g K x the cup's last temperature to warm from 0 C; the rest melted the 20 g. IAPWS: 333.4 J/g at 0 C. A little heat reaches the cup through its foam.
